headline_marked: Steam Hardware Distributor [[CEVA Logistics]] Hit by Cyberattack, Valve Warns Users
headline: Steam Hardware Distributor CEVA Logistics Hit by Cyberattack, Valve Warns Users
summary: Personal information and hardware purchase details of Steam customers in Europe were compromised in a cyberattack on Valve's distributor, CEVA Logistics.
details: Valve has alerted Steam hardware customers in Europe to "expect fake messages" via email, SMS, or phone following a cyberattack on its European hardware distributor, CEVA Logistics. The breach occurred between July 29 and August 1, 2026, with hackers gaining access to customer data on August 7.

The compromised data includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and details about the type and price of products ordered. CEVA Logistics retains this information for 90 days to cover order fulfillment. Crucially, sensitive data such as payment information, passwords, and Steam Guard codes were not affected by the attack.

Valve advises customers who purchased Steam hardware, such as the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, in Europe recently to be vigilant. Attackers may attempt to impersonate Steam, Valve, or delivery companies to solicit fake customs or delivery fees, or direct users to fraudulent login portals.

Customers are urged to verify communication URLs carefully. Official Steam support is exclusively at help.steampowered.com, and logins should only occur via store.steampowered.com, www.steampowered.com, steamcommunity.com, or help.steampowered.com. Valve also emphasizes that Steam Support and couriers will never ask for passwords or Steam Guard codes.
CEVA Logistics has since isolated the affected systems, notified data protection authorities, and engaged external investigators to address the cyberattack.

headline: AI Data Centers Face Growing Opposition as Over 70% of Americans Oppose Buildouts
summary: Protests intensify against AI infrastructure projects, with nearly 40 arrests this year as backlash to AI factory buildouts grows.
details: Public opposition to data center construction is surging, with residents, local politicians, and organizers actively pushing back against AI infrastructure projects. Despite arrests of some protestors, the movement continues with rallies and town hall meetings.

In Nashville, a city council measure was approved to block a $700 million data center planned near the local zoo. This action, supported by Mayor Freddie O'Connell, demonstrates a growing trend of local governments intervening against these developments.

Concerns about data centers include water shortages, potential contamination, increased electricity costs for residents, and health issues linked to constant noise. These issues have fueled a significant shift in public opinion, with over 70% of Americans now opposing new data centers near their homes.

The backlash has led to concrete actions, with nearly 70 jurisdictions nationwide blocking new data center builds, some permanently. This widespread resistance is forcing developers and governments to reconsider the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

The protests have not been without consequence, as close to 40 individuals have been arrested this year for pushing back against data center rollouts. Incidents range from exceeding speaking time at meetings to clapping after a statement, highlighting the tension between protestors and authorities.

Despite the opposition, data center builders continue to advocate for their projects, leveraging government influence and public platforms to promote AI and data center expansion. However, the grassroots movement is demonstrating its power to influence policy and halt construction.
